claim: Epithelial tissues of the developing embryos elongate by different mechanisms, such as neighbor exchange, cell elongation, and oriented cell division.
source: Epithelial tissues of the developing embryos elongate by different mechanisms, such as neighbor exchange, cell elongation, and oriented cell division.
evidence: This is a general statement about epithelial tissue elongation mechanisms that is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Global elongation of epithelial colonies happens primarily due to cell elongations.
source: By quantifying deformation kinematics at multiple scales, we report that global elongation happens primarily due to cell elongations, and its direction correlates with the anisotropy of the average cell elongation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from shear decomposition analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The direction of global elongation correlates with the anisotropy of the average cell elongation.
source: By quantifying deformation kinematics at multiple scales, we report that global elongation happens primarily due to cell elongations, and its direction correlates with the anisotropy of the average cell elongation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing correlation between mean nematic orientation and colony elongation direction in Figure 5.

claim: By imposing an external time-periodic stretch, the axis of global symmetry breaking can be modified.
source: By imposing an external time-periodic stretch, the axis of this global symmetry breaking can be modified and elongation occurs primarily due to orientated neighbor exchange.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cyclic stretching experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Under external time-periodic stretch, elongation occurs primarily due to oriented neighbor exchange.
source: By imposing an external time-periodic stretch, the axis of this global symmetry breaking can be modified and elongation occurs primarily due to orientated neighbor exchange.
evidence: This is supported by shear decomposition analysis of stretched colonies shown in Figure 6e-f.

claim: Rearrangement of neighboring cells or T1 transitions is essential in the germ band extension of Drosophila.
source: Rearrangement of neighboring cells or T1 transitions is essential in the germ band extension of Drosophila (Rauzi et al., 2008; Rauzi et al., 2010), allowing a group of cells to change their position by intercalation, eventually leading to tissue elongation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on Drosophila development.

claim: Cell deformation drives the threefold elongation process in C. elegans.
source: Cell deformation drives the threefold elongation process in C. elegans (Ciarletta et al., 2009; Vuong-Brender, 2016) while keeping the number of cells and their positions fixed.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on C. elegans development.

claim: Epithelial spreading during zebrafish epiboly is promoted by oriented cell divisions as a mechanism to limit tension.
source: Finally, epithelial spreading during zebrafish epiboly is promoted by oriented cell divisions as a mechanism to limit tension (Campinho et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on zebrafish development.

claim: Large colonies (750 µm in diameter) expanded isotropically.
source: We observed that large colonies (750 µm in diameter) expanded isotropically (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Colonies of 250 µm in diameter expanded in a non-isotropic manner.
source: In contrast, colonies of 250 µm in diameter (Figure 1b), the typical coherence length of such epithelial tissues (Doxzen et al., 2013), expanded in a non-isotropic manner (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b-c and by citation to previous work on coherence length.

claim: 250 µm is the typical coherence length of epithelial tissues.
source: In contrast, colonies of 250 µm in diameter (Figure 1b), the typical coherence length of such epithelial tissues (Doxzen et al., 2013), expanded in a non-isotropic manner (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: MDCK colonies elongated persistently along the main axis of elongation for 6 hr.
source: As can be seen in Figure 1e, MDCK colonies elongated persistently along the main axis of elongation (Qxx > 0 and Qxy ≈ 0) for 6 hr (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Circular epithelial colonies of Caco2 and MCF-10A cells elongated along the main axis of elongation by the same magnitude as MDCK cells.
source: Circular epithelial colonies of human epithelial colorectal adenocarcinoma cells (Caco2) and human mammary epithelial cells (MCF-10A) also elongated along the main axis of elongation and by the same magnitude that MDCK cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Elongation observed during 6 hours for the three epithelial cell lines was similar in magnitude to tissue elongation observed during in vivo morphogenesis in the wing blade in Drosophila.
source: We note that elongation observed during this time for the three epithelial cell lines was similar in magnitude to tissue elongation observed during in vivo morphogenesis, for instance in the wing blade in Drosophila (Etournay et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim compares experimental observations to published in vivo data.

claim: The elongation direction converges to a constant value within 2 hr after stencil removal.
source: Moreover, the elongation direction (θfinal = θ (t = 6 h)) converges to a constant value within 2 hr after t0 (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Mechanical cycles of contraction-relaxation can range from 1 s in C. elegans epithelial elongation up to 200 s in dorsal closure.
source: Mechanical cycles of contraction-relaxation can range from 1 s in C. elegans epithelial elongation (Zhang et al., 2011) up to 200 s in dorsal closure (Solon et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Colony elongation along the direction imposed by the external strain was observed when stretched cyclically with 60 s timescale and 5% strain.
source: Among different conditions, we observed colony elongation along the direction imposed by the external strain when we stretched cyclically with 60 s timescale and 5% strain (Figure 2b and Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and Video 3.

claim: The overall elongation of colonies under cyclic uniaxial stretching was similar to the spontaneous elongation in the absence of externally applied uniaxial stretching during the first 2 hr.
source: The overall elongation of colonies under cyclic uniaxial stretching was similar to the spontaneous elongation in the absence of externally applied uniaxial stretching during the first 2 hr (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Single MDCK cells oriented perpendicularly to the externally applied uniaxial cyclic stretching.
source: We observed that cells oriented perpendicularly to the externally applied uniaxial cyclic stretching (Figure 3a and b) as previously reported for fibroblasts (Faust et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a-b and by citation to previous work on fibroblasts.

claim: Colonies treated with anti E-cadherin antibody expanded more than control colonies in the absence of externally applied uniaxial cyclic stretching.
source: In the absence of externally applied uniaxial cyclic stretching, colonies treated with anti E-cadherin antibody expanded more than control colonies.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Under cyclic uniaxial stretching, colonies with blocked E-cadherin showed elongation along the direction perpendicular to the cyclic stretching direction.
source: Under cyclic uniaxial stretching, elongation was also non-isotropic and along the direction perpendicular to the cyclic stretching direction, in contrast to the parallel elongation observed when cell-cell contacts were intact (Figure 2b–d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d and comparison to Figure 2b-d.

claim: Cells inside the colony exhibited a decrease in their mean velocity under stretching conditions.
source: It is worth noting that cells inside the colony exhibited a decrease in their mean velocity (Figure 3e) and a large recruitment of myosin within cells similar to reinforcements (Riveline et al., 2001) in stretching conditions, as shown by the appearance of stress fibers (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e-f and by citation to previous work on reinforcements.

claim: Cells showed large recruitment of myosin within cells similar to reinforcements in stretching conditions, as shown by the appearance of stress fibers.
source: It is worth noting that cells inside the colony exhibited a decrease in their mean velocity (Figure 3e) and a large recruitment of myosin within cells similar to reinforcements (Riveline et al., 2001) in stretching conditions, as shown by the appearance of stress fibers (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f and by citation to previous work.

claim: An acto-myosin cable, similar to compartmentalization boundaries in vivo, was observed in the outer boundary of the colonies at stencil removal.
source: In most of the experiments, an acto-myosin cable, similar to compartmentalization boundaries in vivo (Monier et al., 2010; Calzolari et al., 2014), was observed in the outer boundary of the colonies at stencil removal (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and by citations to previous work on compartmentalization boundaries.

claim: When the supra-cellular acto-myosin cable is intact, cells at the periphery undergo clockwise and counter clockwise rotations.
source: When this supra-cellular structure is intact, cells at the periphery are reported to undergo clockwise and counter clockwise rotations (Doxzen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: When a local interruption of the acto-myosin cable appeared, the cell at the vicinity could extend a lamellipodia and move away radially from the center of the colony.
source: In contrast, when a local interruption of this cable appeared, the cell at the vicinity could extend a lamellipodia and move away and radially from the center of the colony (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: A local defect in the acto-myosin cable could promote the local protrusion of a cell in the direction normal to the edge.
source: Apparently, a local defect in the cable could promote the local protrusion of a cell in the direction normal to the edge as shown in laser ablation experiments previously (Reffay et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from current observations and citation to previous laser ablation experiments.

claim: The elongation direction of the whole colony correlated on average with the direction of the leader cell migration and associated finger.
source: We could observe that the elongation direction of the whole colony correlated on average with the direction of the leader cell migration and associated finger (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: When growing perpendicular to the direction of force application, finger cells performed shorter displacements than when growing parallel to it.
source: We observed that, when growing perpendicular to the direction of force application, finger cells performed shorter displacements than when growing parallel to it.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: When fingers were growing perpendicular to the stretching direction, they shrank upon application of cyclic uniaxial stretching.
source: When fingers were growing perpendicular to the stretching direction, they shrank upon application of cyclic uniaxial stretching; in contrast, fingers further elongated when parallel to the direction of uniaxial cyclic stretching.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Fingers further elongated when parallel to the direction of uniaxial cyclic stretching.
source: When fingers were growing perpendicular to the stretching direction, they shrank upon application of cyclic uniaxial stretching; in contrast, fingers further elongated when parallel to the direction of uniaxial cyclic stretching.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Breakage of the acto-myosin cable by laser ablation induces the appearance of leader cells.
source: Breakage of the acto-myosin cable by laser ablation induces the appearance of leader cells (Reffay et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Transient injection of cytochalasin D was followed by the disruption of the acto-myosin cable, but the cable reformed and fingers did not appear.
source: The transient injection of this actin polymerization inhibitor was followed by the disruption of the acto-myosin cable (Video 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1). However, the cable reformed, and fingers did not appear.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Video 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Breakage of the cable alone does not trigger the growth of fingers in the colonies.
source: This result shows that breakage of the cable alone does not trigger the growth of fingers in our colonies, and suggests that other mechanisms may be involved.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cytochalasin D experiment results.

claim: When a finger moves outward from the colony, cells in the immediate vicinity elongate and seem to reorient their elongation axis toward the finger.
source: We observed that when a finger moves outward from the colony, cells in the immediate vicinity elongate and seem to reorient their elongation axis toward the finger (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Topological defects in the cell elongation nematic field have a key role on epithelial dynamics.
source: Recent studies have shown that the nematic field of cell elongation and its topological defects could be involved in the growth of bacterial colonies (Doostmohammadi et al., 2016) and in controlling dynamics, death and extrusion of epithelial cells (Kawaguchi et al., 2017; Mueller et al., 2019; Saw et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There was a clear average cell elongation even at the time of stencil removal t0.
source: Strikingly, we observed a clear average cell elongation even at the time of stencil removal t0, and the corresponding angle θnematic correlated with colony orientation when elongation direction was established for both MDCK and MCF 10A cell lines (Figure 5d, Figure 5—figure supplement 2d and e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 2d-e.

claim: The angle θnematic of average cell elongation at t0 correlated with colony orientation when elongation direction was established for both MDCK and MCF 10A cell lines.
source: Strikingly, we observed a clear average cell elongation even at the time of stencil removal t0, and the corresponding angle θnematic correlated with colony orientation when elongation direction was established for both MDCK and MCF 10A cell lines (Figure 5d, Figure 5—figure supplement 2d and e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 2d-e.

claim: The location of finger nucleation seemed to be biased toward the position of topological defects.
source: Moreover, the location of finger nucleation seemed to be biased toward the position of topological defects.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations, though the authors note limitations to this interpretation.

claim: The mean nematic direction is a better readout for the cell-shape nematic field than defect positions.
source: However, some defect locations were not stable in time and in some cases, the nematic field of cell shapes could only be interpreted in terms of virtual defects outside the colonies, thus suggesting that the mean nematic direction is a better readout for the cell-shape nematic field.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of defect stability and location.

claim: There was no correlation between breaks of the acto-myosin cable surrounding the colony and the mean nematic direction.
source: Moreover, we found no correlation between breaks of the acto-myosin cable surrounding the colony and the mean nematic direction (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), which suggests that breaks are uniformly distributed along the colony border.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The orientation of the mean cell-shape nematic of the colony before stencil removal sets the direction of elongation by triggering the growth of fingers.
source: Altogether, our results could indicate that the orientation of the mean cell-shape nematic of the colony before stencil removal sets the direction of elongation by triggering the growth of fingers, which appear at the discontinuities of the outer acto-myosin cable located along the nematic orientation, while preventing finger growth at discontinuities located in other directions.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: The mean cell elongation nematic field of colonies under uniaxial cyclic stretching did not change over time.
source: Finally, when looking at the evolution of the mean cell elongation nematic field of colonies under uniaxial cyclic stretching, we observed that it did not change over time (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Average cell elongation alone does not determine colony elongation direction when subjected to uniaxial cyclic stretching.
source: This suggests that average cell elongation alone does not determine colony elongation direction when subjected to uniaxial cyclic stretching.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mean nematic direction remains constant under stretching while colony elongation direction changes.

claim: The total pure shear from shear decomposition analysis gives values consistent with elongation estimates from ellipse fitting.
source: At the colony scale, shear decomposition plots (Figure 6c and Figure 6—figure supplement 3) revealed that the total pure shear gives values consistent with elongation estimates from ellipse fitting (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data from two different analysis methods shown in Figure 6c-d.

claim: After the first 2 hr, the contribution of cell elongation is generally comparable to the total pure shear for control colonies.
source: However, we found that after the first 2 hr, the contribution of cell elongation is generally comparable to the total pure shear, with a smaller contribution from other sources (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is supported by shear decomposition data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: For colonies under cyclic uniaxial stretching, shear created by T1 transitions is the main contributor for the total pure shear.
source: Interestingly, we found however that in that case, shear created by T1 transitions is the main contributor for the total pure shear, while cell elongation does not contribute to tissue elongation (Figure 6f and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by shear decomposition data for stretched colonies shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Applying oscillatory forces to the tissue changes fundamentally the main mode of tissue elongation by favoring topological rearrangements of the cell network.
source: This indicates that applying oscillatory forces to the tissue changes fundamentally the main mode of tissue elongation by favoring topological rearrangements of the cell network.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of shear decomposition between control and stretched colonies.

claim: The vertex model simulations reproduce experimental observations indicating that colony deformation can be understood without forces exerted by a leader cell at the colony boundary.
source: Upon removal of confinement, we found that the simulated colony spontaneously elongates, in a direction set by the orientation of the mean cell elongation nematic field, along with the formation of finger-like structures near the +½ defect, as observed experimentally (see Video 8). Our simulations therefore reproduce experimental observations indicating that colony deformation can be understood without forces exerted by a leader cell at the colony boundary (Figure 7c, Video 8, and Appendix 2).
evidence: This is supported by vertex model simulations shown in Figure 7c and Video 8.

claim: When cellular active stress σa was dominant in the model, the colony elongation was primarily due to cell elongation.
source: When σa was dominant, the colony elongation was primarily due to cell elongation, whereas when λ was the stronger term, T1 transitions were the main cause of colony elongation.
evidence: This is supported by vertex model simulations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: When edge tension bias λ was the stronger term in the model, T1 transitions were the main cause of colony elongation.
source: When σa was dominant, the colony elongation was primarily due to cell elongation, whereas when λ was the stronger term, T1 transitions were the main cause of colony elongation.
evidence: This is supported by vertex model simulations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: When cell-cell junctions are intact, colony elongation is along the direction of stretching and through T1 transitions.
source: When cell-cell junctions are intact, colony elongation is along the direction of stretching and through T1 transitions (Figure 2c and Figure 6f), suggesting that the tendency of single cells to orient along y (Figure 3a–b) is partially screened by cell-cell junctions via T1 transitions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c and Figure 6f, and by inference from model simulations.

claim: When cell-cell junctions are weakened, active cell stress dominates, and colonies elongate perpendicular to the uniaxial stretching direction.
source: When cell-cell junctions are weakened, active cell stress dominates, and colonies, which could be thought of to be closer to a collection of single cells, elongate perpendicular to the uniaxial stretching direction (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c-d and by inference from model simulations.

claim: ROCK is involved in cell-cell contacts integrity in vivo.
source: We perturbed active stress and line edge tension by inhibiting ROCK, which has been reported to be involved in cell-cell contact integrity in vivo (Nishimura and Takeichi, 2008; Ewald et al., 2012), and recently, in cell responses to stretching in vitro (Hart, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ROCK is involved in cell responses to stretching in vitro.
source: We perturbed active stress and line edge tension by inhibiting ROCK, which has been reported to be involved in cell-cell contact integrity in vivo (Nishimura and Takeichi, 2008; Ewald et al., 2012), and recently, in cell responses to stretching in vitro (Hart, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: When ROCK activity is inhibited, colonies under uniaxial stretching elongate through single-cell elongation rather than T1 transitions.
source: Strikingly, the application of a ROCK inhibitor leads to single-cell elongation dominating over T1 (orange dot in Figure 8c), effectively suppressing the effect of uniaxial cyclic stretching on the mode of colony deformation (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Symmetry breaking and finger formation in colonies and the corresponding tissue kinematics observed in experiments could be brought about by collective active behavior of the colony cells and does not require special action of leader cells.
source: From our simulations, we could demonstrate that symmetry breaking and finger formation in colonies and the corresponding tissue kinematics observed in our experiments could be brought about by collective active behavior of the colony cells and does not require special action of leader cells (Theveneau and Linker, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by vertex model simulations and comparison to experimental data.

claim: Cell-level internal activities and cell-cell interactions are sufficient to cause symmetry breaking in the colony shape and its overall kinematics via the collective cell-shape nematic field.
source: Thus, although leader cells at the boundary may play a role in the border fingering, our experimental findings and simulations clearly indicate that the cell-level internal activities and cell-cell interactions are sufficient to cause symmetry breaking in the colony shape and its overall kinematics via the collective cell-shape nematic field.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and model simulations.

claim: Circular epithelial colonies when in confinement build up a mean nematic orientation that results from the inner activity of cells and sets the direction for colony elongation.
source: Now, we showed that circular epithelial colonies when in confinement build up a mean nematic orientation. This symmetry breaking results from the inner activity of cells, and sets the direction for colony elongation.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings presented throughout the paper.

claim: MDCK cells assume features of epithelial cells in vivo, such as adherens junctions, cytoskeletal components, and the Rho signaling pathway regulating cell shapes and dynamics.
source: We prepared isotropic colonies of Madin Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK) cells, which assume features of epithelial cells in vivo (Reinsch and Karsenti, 1994; Adams et al., 1998; Reffay et al., 2014), such as adherens junctions (Adams et al., 1998), cytoskeletal components, and the Rho signaling pathway regulating cell shapes and dynamics (Reffay et al., 2014; Fodor et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work characterizing MDCK cells.

claim: Leader cells at the boundary are on average faster than other boundary cells.
source: We performed cell tracking and observed that, on average, these protruding cells are faster than other boundary cells (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 2b-c.

claim: Leader cells are characterized by radial and directional migrations, in contrast to tangential motion observed in the other cells of the outer region of the colony.
source: They are characterized also by radial and directional migrations, in contrast to tangential motion observed in the other cells of the outer region of the colony (Figure 4—figure supplement 2d and e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2d-e.

claim: The motion of leader cells was directionally persistent and on average the shape of the whole colony followed the same overall direction.
source: In general, the motion of these so-called leader cells was directionally persistent and on average the shape of the whole colony followed the same overall direction (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b-c.

claim: In the absence of externally applied cyclic uniaxial stretching, fingers grew a similar amount as when growing parallel the direction of applied uniaxial cyclic stretching and no bias was observed vis-à-vis the nucleation position.
source: In the absence of externally applied cyclic uniaxial stretching, fingers grew a similar amount as when growing parallel the direction of applied uniaxial cyclic stretching and no bias was observed vis-à-vis the nucleation position (Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2f.

claim: The defect position and strength can be used to provide an approximate readout for the orientation of the cell-shape nematic field.
source: Thus, the defect position and strength can be used to provide an approximate readout for the orientation of the cell-shape nematic field (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by theoretical analysis and comparison to experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The initial mean direction of cell elongation, either parallel or perpendicular to the external stretching, was maintained throughout 2 hr of external stretching.
source: The initial mean direction of cell elongation, either parallel or perpendicular to the external stretching, was maintained throughout 2 hr of external stretching.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Some of the colonies exhibit shear decomposition patterns similar to those observed during Drosophila pupal wing elongation.
source: We also systematically quantified the shear deformation kinematics of the colony and demonstrated that some of the colonies exhibit shear decomposition patterns similar to those observed during Drosophila pupal wing elongation (Etournay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental data to published in vivo data.

claim: Cell anisotropic active stress results mainly in cell elongation.
source: Specifically, we showed that cell anisotropic active stress results mainly in cell elongation, whereas anisotropies in cortical contractility primarily effects cell intercalations or T1 transitions.
evidence: This is supported by vertex model simulations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Anisotropies in cortical contractility primarily affect cell intercalations or T1 transitions.
source: Specifically, we showed that cell anisotropic active stress results mainly in cell elongation, whereas anisotropies in cortical contractility primarily effects cell intercalations or T1 transitions.
evidence: This is supported by vertex model simulations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Including cell motilities appears to enhance tissue shear generated by the other two modes of internal forcing.
source: Including cell motilities appears to enhance tissue shear generated by the other two modes of internal forcing.
evidence: This is supported by vertex model simulations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: When ROCK is inhibited, colonies under uniaxial stretching shifted from primarily elongating through cell intercalations to a single cell elongation driven mechanism.
source: By doing so, colonies which primarily elongate through cell intercalations, shifted to a single cell elongation driven mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: When cyclic stretching was applied to colonies treated with ROCK inhibitor, elongation along the direction of the uniaxial cyclic stretching was absent.
source: When cyclic stretching was applied, elongation along the direction of the uniaxial cyclic stretching was absent (Qxx ≈ Qxy) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1a-b.

claim: Colonies treated with ROCK inhibitor still elongated anisotropically under cyclic stretching, similar to colonies in the absence of application of uniaxial cyclic stretching.
source: However, colonies still elongated anisotropically, similar to colonies in the absence of application of uniaxial cyclic stretching (Figure 8—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1c.

claim: A competition between the strength of active T1 transitions parallel to the external stretching and active cell stress perpendicular to the external stretching dictate overall colony elongation under uniaxial cyclic stretching.
source: Therefore, we propose that a competition between the strength of active T1 transitions parallel to the external stretching and active cell stress perpendicular to the external stretching dictate overall colony elongation under uniaxial cyclic stretching.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on integration of experimental and modeling results.
